title: Cervical, Brachial, and Lumbosacral Plexuses
subtitle: Telling a plexus lesion (several nerves, several roots) from a single nerve or root lesion, and placing it in trunk, cord or plexus level

points.text: The cervical plexus is made of the anterior rami of C1-C4.
points.quote: The cervical plexus, formed by the anterior primary rami of C1-C4

points.text: C1 has no dorsal root, so it is purely motor.
points.quote: there is no dorsal root from C1; therefore, C1 is a purely motor root

points.text: The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) carries sensation from the lower cheek over the mandible and the lower external ear.
points.quote: skin of the lower cheek over the mandible, the lower part of the external ear, and the upper neck below the external ear

points.text: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) supplies the diaphragm.
points.quote: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5), which innervates the diaphragm

points.text: The plexus is built from roots, trunks, divisions, cords and branches, in that proximal-to-distal order.
points.quote: It is divided into five major components (in a proximal to distal direction): roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and branches

points.text: C5 and C6 form the upper trunk, C7 the middle trunk, and C8-T1 the lower trunk.
points.quote: The fifth and sixth cervical roots course downward between the scalenus medius and anterior muscles and unite to form the upper trunk

points.text: The anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks make the lateral cord; the lower trunk makes the medial cord; the three posterior divisions make the posterior cord.
points.quote: The anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks (C5-C7) unite to form the lateral cord

points.text: Some branches leave directly from roots or trunk: the long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) supplies serratus anterior, the suprascapular nerve (C5-C6) supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
points.quote: The long thoracic nerve arises directly from C5-C7 roots and descends vertically behind the plexus to innervate the serratus anterior muscle.

points.text: Posterior cord branches: subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves.
points.quote: (b) the thoracodorsal nerve (C5-C8), (c) the axillary nerve (C5-C6), and (d) the radial nerve (C5-C8)

points.text: The plexus lies within the psoas major, formed by T12 through S4 ventral rami.
points.quote: derives from the ventral primary rami of the 12th thoracic through 4th sacral levels

points.text: Prefixed or postfixed derivations occur in up to 20% of healthy subjects.
points.quote: Anomalous derivations of the plexus (prefixed or postfixed) occur in up to 20% of healthy subjects.

points.text: A complete lumbar plexus lesion mainly involves the femoral and obturator motor distributions.
points.quote: There is paresis and atrophy, predominantly in the motor distributions of the femoral and obturator nerves.

points.text: A sacral plexus lesion involves the superior gluteal, inferior gluteal and sciatic nerves.
points.quote: Lesions of the sacral plexus result in motor disturbances in the field of distribution of the superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, and sciatic nerves.

localizationRules.rule: A plexopathy involves more than one nerve
localizationRules.explanation: The hallmark is a deficit that cannot be explained by a single root or peripheral nerve; in the leg the same logic applies, with pain plus sensorimotor deficits in several nerve distributions.
localizationRules.quote: The most prominent sign of a brachial plexopathy is a clinical deficit that involves more than one spinal or peripheral nerve.

localizationRules.explanation: Upper plexus lesions involve C5-C6 or the upper trunk; lower plexus lesions involve C8-T1 or the lower trunk, so the pattern of weak muscles and sensory loss points to the level.
localizationRules.quote: a lesion that results from damage to the fifth and sixth cervical roots or the upper trunk of the brachial plexus

localizationRules.rule: Cord lesions follow the cord's branches
localizationRules.explanation: Lateral cord: musculocutaneous and lateral median head; medial cord: ulnar and medial median head; posterior cord: subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions of the posterior cord result in disability in the fields of distribution of the subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary, and radial nerves.

localizationRules.rule: Phrenic palsy usually points below the plexus
localizationRules.explanation: Phrenic damage more often comes from a mediastinal process than from the cervical plexus; ask about neck or chest surgery, catheters and mass lesions.
localizationRules.quote: Unilateral or bilateral damage to the phrenic nerve is more often caused by a mediastinal process than by damage to the cervical plexus itself.

localizationRules.explanation: Pain with sensory and motor deficits spread over multiple spinal and peripheral nerve territories of one leg suggests the plexus rather than a root or a single nerve.
localizationRules.quote: A lumbosacral plexopathy is recognized by pain and sensorimotor deficits in the distribution of multiple spinal and peripheral nerves in the lower extremity.

keySyndromes.name: Upper plexus paralysis (Erb-Duchenne)
keySyndromes.triad: Paralysis of deltoid, biceps, brachioradialis and brachialis (C5-C6) + limb internally rotated and adducted with forearm extended and pronated (policeman's or porter's tip) + biceps and brachioradialis reflexes depressed or absent + sensory loss, if any, over the outer upper arm
keySyndromes.clue: Damage to C5-C6 or the upper trunk; sensation is usually intact and the triceps is spared.
keySyndromes.quote: the limb is internally rotated and adducted, and the forearm is extended and pronated

keySyndromes.name: Lower plexus paralysis (Dejerine-Klumpke)
keySyndromes.triad: Weak wrist and finger flexion + weak intrinsic hand muscles with claw hand + sensory loss on medial arm, medial forearm and ulnar hand + finger flexor reflex (C8-T1) depressed + ipsilateral Horner syndrome if T1 is injured
keySyndromes.clue: C8-T1 roots or lower trunk; associated with arm traction in abduction and with Pancoast tumor or aortic arch aneurysm.
keySyndromes.quote: Therefore, there is weakness of wrist and finger flexion and weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles. Often, a claw hand deformity is evident.

keySyndromes.name: Neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner)
keySyndromes.triad: Acute severe shoulder pain radiating to arm, neck and back + paresis of shoulder and proximal arm muscles within hours to days + sensory loss generally not marked + arm held flexed at the elbow and adducted (flexion-adduction sign)
keySyndromes.clue: Axillary, suprascapular, radial, musculocutaneous and long thoracic nerves are most affected; phrenic palsy may occur; because of C5-C6 innervation it often mimics an upper plexus lesion.
keySyndromes.quote: acute, severe pain located in the shoulder and radiating into the arm, neck, and back

keySyndromes.name: Total plexus paralysis
keySyndromes.triad: Entire arm paralyzed and limp with rapid atrophy + complete anesthesia distal to an oblique line from the tip of the shoulder to halfway down the medial arm + areflexic upper extremity
keySyndromes.clue: Rare; usually severe trauma such as a fall from a moving vehicle.
keySyndromes.quote: The entire arm is paralyzed and hangs limp at the patient's side.

keySyndromes.name: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Pain (often intermittent) in the ulnar border of the hand and the medial forearm and arm + paresthesias and sensory loss in the same area + motor and reflex findings of a lower plexus palsy
keySyndromes.clue: Involvement may be restricted to C8 fibers, giving thenar wasting (median) with ulnar-supplied muscles spared; the true neurogenic form is extremely rare.
keySyndromes.quote: Usually, the lower trunk or medial cord of the brachial plexus is involved.

keySyndromes.name: Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy (diabetic amyotrophy)
keySyndromes.triad: Subacute painful asymmetric lower limb neuropathy + weight loss + type 2 diabetes mellitus + progression to widespread bilateral paralytic disorder
keySyndromes.clue: Nondiabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy is clinically similar; both show ischemic injury and microvasculitis in cutaneous nerves.
keySyndromes.quote: a well-recognized subacute, painful, asymmetric lower limb neuropathy that is associated with weight loss and type 2 diabetes mellitus

boardTraps.text: A patient whose deficit does not fit the usual pattern may have a prefixed or postfixed plexus (one-level shift, 3% to 5% of patients).
boardTraps.quote: must be considered in any patient who does not fit the usual clinical presentation of a brachial plexopathy

boardTraps.text: A phrenic nerve may receive an anastomotic branch from the subclavian nerve, so diaphragmatic action can be normal even after a proximal phrenic lesion.
boardTraps.quote: diaphragmatic action may be normal after a proximal phrenic lesion

boardTraps.text: Metastatic plexopathy tends to affect the lower trunk with early severe pain and Horner syndrome; radiation plexopathy tends to affect the upper trunk or whole plexus with paresthesias and weakness before pain. The book notes that some authors found no anatomic difference.
boardTraps.quote: With metastatic disease, the lower trunk (C8-T1) is predominantly or exclusively involved, severe pain is present at onset, and Horner syndrome is common.

boardTraps.text: Positioning injuries in anesthesia are mainly stretch injuries; upper plexus lesions occur with full arm abduction and lower plexus lesions when the arm is close to the side.
boardTraps.quote: Stretch of nerve fibers, rather than compression, is the chief cause of injury

boardTraps.text: In a middle trunk (C7) lesion the extensors of forearm, hand and fingers are weak but forearm flexion is spared.
boardTraps.quote: Forearm flexion is spared because the brachioradialis and brachialis are innervated predominantly by the fifth and sixth cervical segments.

boardTraps.text: Radial pulse obliteration with the arm abducted and externally rotated is not specific for thoracic outlet syndrome, since healthy people can show it.
boardTraps.quote: the radial pulse is frequently obliterated; however, pulse obliteration is occasionally seen in healthy individuals
